18.t: Joe Garland and In the Mood
18.s: He says Joe Garland wrote In the Mood and Leapfrog and made Glenn Miller popular, though the public credits Miller.
18.ch: Union, publishers, race and Harlem nightlife
18.q: Glenn didn't. I mean that's what the public thinks.

18.t: Tommy Dorsey's playing and Glenn Miller's In the Mood
18.s: He heard Dorsey play like no one but himself; they argue Joe Garland made Glenn Miller famous with In the Mood.
18.q: Joe Garland wrote it; Edgar Hayes played it. Edgar Hayes was the first musician - you know Edgar Hayes; he's my girl friend's husband. They live out in California. We all came up together. Edgar Hayes wanted to buy that music. When I lived down on ( ) Seventh Avenue he lived down there too, he and…

7.t: Writing the 'Minnie the Moocher' introduction overnight
7.s: Cab asked for an arrangement; Thomas wrote an eight-bar intro and ending on strips of paper.
7.q: So we was going down to record the next day, and that night before we was going to record the next day, Cab came to me and said, "Foots, make an arrangement on 'Minnie The Moocher.'" Because I had heard it two or three times, and I'd seen it.

7.t: 'Hi-De-Ho', 'Willie the Weeper' and how Foots wrote the 'Minnie the Moocher' arrangement
7.s: Mills adapted the public-domain 'Willie the Weeper' as 'Minnie the Moocher'; Cab asked Thomas to fix a failed arrangement and he wrote the intro overnight, echoing 'Get Happy'.
7.q: "Hi-Di-Ho" was a public domain song named "Willie The Weeper." And Mills got Parrish to write the words to "Minnie The Moocher"... He took the same lyrics and the same melody, and made it "Minnie The Moocher." That's a story within itself. So we got this arrangement... I wish I could think of that…

33.t: Stock arrangements, X-20 medley and band jokes
33.s: DeDroit discusses imitation, pasting phrases into arrangements, the X-20 medley and some band mishaps with Benny and Freddie Newman.
33.q: Well I guess it's a compliment. Well that is a compliment. I know that imitation is a height of flattering. Maybe I unconsciously stole some things too, you know. Anything that's successful is worthwhile listening to. But I've realized that stock arrangements, every band would sound alike if you…

256.t: Wingy Manone, In a Mood and money
256.s: He claims Wingy wrote the riff behind In the Mood and collected from Glenn Miller.
256.ch: New Orleans Rhythm Kings and Tin Roof Blues
256.q: And he got a lot of money out of that from Glenn Miller. He didn't. Wingy's a pretty shrewd boy when it comes to money. Yeah. He acts illiterate but he's pretty smart. He's like Maxie Rosenblum. Yeah. Musical Maxie Rosenblum.

604.t: Glenn Miller's hits and the origin of 'Moonlight Serenade'
604.s: From the Miller archives he recounts how 'Glenn's Theme' was written as a Schillinger exercise and Ray Noble turned down the clarinet-lead sound.
604.q: And he was remarkable. Because it seemed like he really knew how to turn out hit records. He did. One after another. I can’t think of any other band that has as many hit recordings as Glenn Miller.

996.t: Altered tunings, Dan Foliart and Henry Worrall's Spanish Fandango
996.s: Juber describes notation for altered tunings with Dan Foliart and the history from Worrall to open G tuning and 'Honky Tonk Woman'.
996.q: Well that particular composer, Dan Foliart, who I’ve worked with for over 30 years, he did “Roseanne,” “Home Improvement,” a lot of shows. We did a show for 11 years called “Seventh Heaven” where the acoustic guitar was extremely prominent. Finger style acoustic guitar. And he was always write in…

348.t: Les Brown's classical-themed hits and Sentimental Journey
348.s: Brown's band used classical adaptations like Mexican Hat Dance; Ben Homer really wrote Sentimental Journey.
348.q: Yes. Well Les was — it was mainly a hard swing band I thought. And what he tried to do was take some of the classical things, like “March Slave,” “Mexican Hat Dance,” and things like that, which fortunately I had some clarinet solos to play in those. And he did quite well with those. And then he…

62.t: Yard Dog Mazurka with Roger Segure and the Lunceford draw
62.s: Wilson tells how Yard Dog Mazurka was written, co-credited to Roger Segure, and became a Lunceford hit, and why Lunceford's band could outdraw any other.
62.q: Okay, okay I’ll tell you how that happens. Roger Segure was a fine young writer who was with the Lunceford band. He was also – wrote for Louis Armstrong, and for many acts. He actually wrote at – he was actually working with a lot of the acts and people out of the Joe Glazer office. Okay he was…

109.t: "In the Mood": Joe Garland, Eddie Durham and the 1936 recording
109.s: Garland wrote "In the Mood"; Clarke gave it to Eddie Durham for Glenn Miller, and Hayes's band had recorded it years earlier.
109.q: So he asked me, 'Hey, Kenny, any new things? Because I'm writing. I need all the music I can get.' And I brought him, 'In the Mood.'

137.t: Wham and giving Glenn Miller half the credit
137.s: Wham was written for Moten, reworked for lyricist Taps Miller, and recorded by Glenn Miller in exchange for half the writer credit.
137.q: Well, here's the way it was. Taps Miller had the lyrics. He went to Basie, Basie wouldn't do them because they was all out of meter and he didn't have the meters, he couldn't fit the words with the music.

230.t: Being offered In the Mood at a Lincoln Hotel rehearsal
230.s: At a 2 a.m. rehearsal in the Blue Room of the Lincoln, a stranger offered an arrangement for his name; Barnet stopped it after 16 bars and sent the man to Glenn Miller: In the Mood.
230.q: Well, yes. First of all, I wanted to say that at all times, when you had a band and you were broadcasting or recording, there were always people bringing tunes to you and saying, 'Look, I'll put your name on it. You can publish it. You can put it in your company. If you'll just play it.' Now, this…

9.t: Smitty later in Erskine Hawkins's band and Tippin' In
9.s: Smitty later played saxophone with Erskine Hawkins and wrote 'Tippin' In'; the interviewer cannot find him in Rust.
9.ch: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
9.q: The next time I saw Smitty, which was years later, he was playing saxophone in Erskine Hawkins' band -- Smitty was. And he was a very good saxophone player. I think he's in California now. Because he went to Europe with...

146.t: Goodman hears the broadcast; Blue Balls renamed One O'Clock Jump
146.s: Smith writes Jack Washington's part, Benny Goodman hears the broadcast and sends John Hammond, and the tune is renamed on air in Little Rock.
146.q: There's too many men blowing, going on (?) for him, and he says, "Well, I can't find a note, Prof." I said, "Well, I'll write you a part out." So I just wrote him a part out. So it got to a point... We were broadcasting that night, 12:30, and Benny Goodman heard it. And he said ...(?). . . "That…

70.t: Erskine Hawkins's band and its head arrangements
70.s: Hawkins's band made up its tunes among themselves, such as Tippin' In and Tuxedo Junction, though credit was disputed.
70.ch: Don Redman's band at Connie's Inn
70.q: Oh, man, it was a beautiful -- Erskine had a good band. They had a lot of head arrangements and they made a lot of tunes up among themselves, you know. That's the way that 'Tippin' In' was made. That's the way 'Tuxedo Junction' was made. There was about three writers to 'Tuxedo Junction' out of the…

103.t: Eddie Durham, Glenn Miller and "Slip Horn Jive" at the Famous Door
103.s: Jones says Eddie Durham took Basie arrangements to Glenn Miller's band, and Miller stopped visiting the Famous Door after Basie played "Slip Horn Jive" without music.
103.q: That's right... He left to go to build Glenn Miller's band. J: He took "Slip Horn Jive" that was a trombone solo that nobody played but Benny Morton and myself, and he made his first big record. He was at the Glen Island Casino.

13.t: Who arranged Rosetta, Angry and Japanese Sandman
13.ch: Swing, singers, Ed Fox and recordings
13.q: I don't know what the heck kind of change I could have made on a Cecil Irwin arrangement. Unless I jazzed it up or something.
